passage:
The formation of long-term memories is widely understood to depend on a process called synaptic consolidation, in which newly acquired information is first encoded as fragile, short-lived changes in the connections between neurons and only later stabilized into durable structural modifications. For decades, the dominant model held that consolidation was essentially a one-time event: once a memory had been stabilized, it was thought to remain permanently fixed unless the brain suffered physical damage. Recent work in cellular neuroscience, however, has fundamentally revised this picture.

The revision centers on a phenomenon known as reconsolidation. When a consolidated memory is reactivated — that is, when a person or animal actively recalls it — the memory transiently returns to a labile, or unstable, state. During this window of instability, the memory becomes vulnerable to disruption by the same molecular interventions that can prevent initial consolidation in the first place. Specifically, drugs that inhibit the synthesis of new proteins, administered during or shortly after reactivation, have been shown in rodent studies to impair the subsequent retrieval of what had been a fully established memory. According to the reconsolidation hypothesis, the brain essentially re-records the memory each time it is recalled, and the re-recording process requires a fresh round of protein synthesis.

The reconsolidation hypothesis carries several intriguing implications. If memories are rendered malleable each time they surface, then recall itself is not a passive read-out but an active reconstruction that updates the stored trace. One implication is that a traumatic memory could, in principle, be weakened by pairing its reactivation with a pharmacological agent that disrupts reconsolidation. Early clinical trials exploring this possibility in patients with post-traumatic stress disorder have produced mixed results: some studies report a modest reduction in the emotional intensity of traumatic recollections, while others detect no significant effect, possibly because the reconsolidation window in humans is narrower or more difficult to target than in laboratory rodents.

Nonetheless, several important questions remain unresolved. It is not yet clear whether all categories of memory undergo reconsolidation or only those encoded under conditions of high emotional salience. Furthermore, the molecular machinery involved — an enzymatic cascade (a series of enzyme-driven chemical reactions, each triggering the next) initiated by a receptor protein on the neuron's surface — has been characterized in detail only in a small number of model systems, and whether these mechanisms operate identically in the human hippocampus is still a matter of active investigation. A more cautious reading of the evidence holds that reconsolidation, whatever its ultimate clinical utility, has already succeeded in dismantling the older notion that consolidated memories are static archives, permanently immune to change.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Research into synaptic consolidation has produced pharmacological tools that are now being used to treat post-traumatic stress disorder in clinical settings.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The reconsolidation hypothesis has overturned the long-held view that consolidated memories are permanently fixed, revealing instead that reactivated memories temporarily become vulnerable to disruption.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Protein-synthesis inhibitors administered during memory reactivation reliably erase traumatic memories in both rodents and humans.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The molecular mechanisms underlying reconsolidation are too poorly understood to support any clinical application of the reconsolidation hypothesis.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Memory reconsolidation demonstrates that the brain re-records every memory each time it is recalled, making long-term memories inherently unreliable.

explanations.correct: The passage introduces the older static-memory view, presents the reconsolidation hypothesis as a fundamental revision, and tracks both its implications and its remaining uncertainties — all organized around the central idea that reactivated memories become temporarily labile, overturning the prior model.
explanations.A: Too narrow and overstated: clinical applications are noted as mixed and exploratory, not as the main subject of the passage.
explanations.B: Correct. This integrates the prior view, the revision, and the key mechanism (lability upon reactivation) across the full passage.
explanations.C: The passage explicitly states clinical results are 'mixed' and questions whether human reconsolidation windows are as accessible as rodent ones — this choice overstates the evidence.
explanations.D: The passage is not primarily negative about clinical prospects; it also notes what reconsolidation has already established. This choice conflates a subordinate caution with the main point.
explanations.E: This overreaches: the passage does not claim memories are 'inherently unreliable,' and the main point concerns the revision of the static-memory model, not a sweeping claim about memory reliability.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A dominant scientific model is introduced, an experimental finding that supports that model is presented, and then the clinical applications of the finding are evaluated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A phenomenon is defined, its molecular mechanism is described in detail, and then its implications for human neurology are shown to be well established.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A long-standing model is introduced and then revised by a competing hypothesis, the implications of the revision are explored, and unresolved questions about its scope and mechanisms are noted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two competing hypotheses about memory are compared, experimental evidence favoring each is presented, and a conclusion about which hypothesis is correct is reached.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A clinical problem involving traumatic memory is described, a proposed molecular solution is analyzed, and the limitations of that solution are shown to outweigh its promise.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces the static-memory model; paragraph 2 presents reconsolidation as a revision; paragraph 3 explores implications (including clinical); paragraph 4 catalogues unresolved questions while affirming what the hypothesis has established.
explanations.A: The experimental finding revises, not supports, the dominant model — this mischaracterizes the relationship.
explanations.B: The molecular mechanism is noted as incompletely understood, not described in full detail; and implications are 'mixed,' not well established.
explanations.C: Correct. This accurately captures the four-paragraph arc.
explanations.D: The passage does not present two hypotheses with balanced evidence and then adjudicate; the reconsolidation hypothesis clearly displaces the older view.
explanations.E: The passage does not start from a clinical problem, and it does not conclude that limitations outweigh promise — the final paragraph is more measured.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, what happens to a consolidated memory during the reconsolidation window?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is permanently erased unless new proteins are synthesized to stabilize it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It becomes temporarily unstable and vulnerable to disruption by protein-synthesis inhibitors.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is transferred from short-term to long-term storage through an enzymatic cascade.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It undergoes structural modification that makes it more resistant to subsequent disruption.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is re-encoded in the hippocampus by the same mechanism that originally produced synaptic consolidation.

explanations.correct: The passage states that upon reactivation the memory 'transiently returns to a labile, or unstable, state' during which protein-synthesis inhibitors can impair subsequent retrieval.
explanations.A: The passage says the memory can be disrupted, not that it is permanently erased; and the directionality is reversed — it is inhibiting protein synthesis that causes impairment.
explanations.B: Correct. This is a close paraphrase of the second paragraph.
explanations.C: The short-to-long-term transfer describes initial synaptic consolidation, not reconsolidation.
explanations.D: The opposite: the memory becomes more vulnerable, not more resistant, during the reconsolidation window.
explanations.E: The passage does not assert that the reconsolidation mechanism is identical to the initial consolidation mechanism; it only notes that protein synthesis is required in both.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that which one of the following is true of the early clinical trials involving reconsolidation and post-traumatic stress disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They were abandoned because protein-synthesis inhibitors proved toxic to human subjects.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Their inconsistent outcomes may reflect a difference between how readily the reconsolidation window can be targeted in humans compared to rodents.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They succeeded in establishing that reconsolidation occurs across all categories of human memory, not only traumatic ones.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They demonstrated conclusively that the emotional intensity of a memory is independent of the molecular reconsolidation process.

choices.label: E
choices.text: They relied primarily on animal models rather than direct observation of human hippocampal activity.

explanations.correct: The passage explains the mixed results 'possibly because the reconsolidation window in humans is narrower or more difficult to target than in laboratory rodents,' directly supporting this inference.
explanations.A: Toxicity is never mentioned; the passage discusses mixed efficacy results, not safety failures.
explanations.B: Correct. This paraphrases the passage's own offered explanation for the mixed outcomes.
explanations.C: The passage raises as an unresolved question whether all memory categories undergo reconsolidation — the trials did not establish this.
explanations.D: The trials showed only mixed and modest reductions; no conclusive independence between emotional intensity and reconsolidation is claimed.
explanations.E: The clinical trials are specifically described as involving patients with PTSD, indicating human subjects, not animal models.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of the enzymatic cascade in the final paragraph serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: demonstrate that reconsolidation has been fully characterized at the molecular level and is ready for clinical translation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: introduce a competing explanation for why consolidated memories can be disrupted upon reactivation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: illustrate one of the open questions about reconsolidation by noting that its molecular underpinnings have been detailed only in limited experimental systems.

choices.label: D
choices.text: explain why protein-synthesis inhibitors are ineffective when administered before rather than during memory reactivation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: provide evidence that the reconsolidation window in humans is longer than in rodents.

explanations.correct: The enzymatic cascade is introduced as part of a list of unresolved questions: it has been 'characterized in detail only in a small number of model systems,' illustrating the limitation that the molecular machinery's human applicability remains uncertain.
explanations.A: The passage says precisely the opposite — the mechanism is not yet confirmed in humans, so clinical translation is not assured.
explanations.B: No competing explanation is introduced; the cascade is presented as the proposed mechanism, not a rival one.
explanations.C: Correct. The mention of the enzymatic cascade exemplifies the broader unresolved question about whether findings from model systems transfer to the human brain.
explanations.D: The timing of administration relative to reactivation is discussed in paragraph 2, not in connection with the enzymatic cascade.
explanations.E: The passage suggests the human window may be narrower, not longer; and this is not the function of the enzymatic cascade discussion.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the reconsolidation hypothesis can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: unreserved enthusiasm for a discovery that has already transformed the treatment of traumatic memory disorders.

choices.label: B
choices.text: cautious endorsement of a well-supported but not yet fully resolved framework that has already displaced an older view.

choices.label: C
choices.text: deep skepticism about whether reconsolidation studies in rodents have any relevance to human memory.

choices.label: D
choices.text: neutral detachment, presenting the hypothesis without committing to any evaluative position.

choices.label: E
choices.text: provisional acceptance contingent on the development of protein-synthesis inhibitors that are safe for human use.

explanations.correct: The author describes reconsolidation as having 'fundamentally revised' the field and as having 'already succeeded in dismantling the older notion' — positive evaluations — while also carefully noting mixed clinical results and unresolved mechanistic questions, indicating a cautiously approving stance.
explanations.A: Overstated: the author notes mixed clinical results and multiple unresolved questions; 'unreserved enthusiasm' misrepresents the measured tone.
explanations.B: Correct. The author affirms the hypothesis's genuine contributions while cataloguing open questions — a hallmark of cautious endorsement.
explanations.C: The passage does not express deep skepticism; it treats rodent findings as legitimately informative while acknowledging translational uncertainty.
explanations.D: The author editorializes explicitly in the final paragraph ('has already succeeded in dismantling'), departing from pure neutrality.
explanations.E: Drug safety is never raised as a prerequisite; the author's qualified approval is not contingent on safety developments.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the reconsolidation hypothesis as described in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Protein-synthesis inhibitors administered to rodents several hours after memory reactivation have no effect on subsequent memory retrieval.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Memories that are recalled frequently in human subjects are subjectively experienced as more vivid than those recalled infrequently.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Studies using a different class of molecular intervention demonstrate that a memory's emotional content can be altered without disrupting its factual content.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rodent studies using rigorous controls show that protein-synthesis inhibitors impair memory retrieval equally whether or not the memory was reactivated before drug administration.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neuroimaging of human subjects during memory recall reveals activation patterns in regions other than the hippocampus.

explanations.correct: The reconsolidation hypothesis depends critically on the claim that the memory's vulnerability to protein-synthesis inhibitors is specifically triggered by reactivation. If the inhibitors impair retrieval equally without reactivation, the link between reactivation-induced lability and protein synthesis is broken, undermining the core mechanism.
explanations.A: This is consistent with the hypothesis: it specifies a time window shortly after reactivation, so effects fading several hours later would actually support the window concept, not undermine it.
explanations.B: Subjective vividness judgments are peripheral to the mechanistic claims of the reconsolidation hypothesis; this has no clear bearing on whether reactivation induces molecular lability.
explanations.C: This concerns a different molecular intervention targeting emotional versus factual content — it does not directly bear on the claim that reactivation renders memories generally labile to protein-synthesis disruption.
explanations.D: Correct. If the protein-synthesis inhibitor is equally destructive regardless of reactivation, the key premise — that reactivation specifically returns a memory to a labile state — is not supported.
explanations.E: The involvement of brain regions beyond the hippocampus does not contradict the claim that reactivated memories become labile; it is off-target with respect to the hypothesis's core assertion.
